挑战T：比较惠更斯号/卡西尼号在土卫六Titan的证据，与新视野号在冥王星和Arrokoth的证据。将着陆点测量与区域/全球遥测区分开。对于沟道、看似活跃的地形和双叶形状，确定观测内容、推断的过程、合理的竞争性解释，以及能够区分这些解释的证据。不要仅凭外观相似直接推断液体成分或现今内部状态。

查找：ESA惠更斯号亮点页面、NASA新视野号页面、Cruikshank等人2020年论文（冥王星地质综述）、McKinnon等人2020年论文（Arrokoth形成），以及关于土卫六湖泊组成、冥王星地质的论文。
assignmentHtml.context: 挑战T需要区分土卫六及冥王星/柯伊伯带天体的直接与间接测量。惠更斯号于2005年1月14日在土卫六着陆（土星的卫星，而非土星本体）。直接测量：大气测量、DISR拍摄的排水沟道与卵石影像、GCMS甲烷信号。沟道由液态甲烷/乙烷切割形成（在-179°C时，水是岩石）。卡西尼号雷达于2006年7月发现湖泊，由甲烷/乙烷组成。新视野号：2015年7月14日飞越冥王星（并非轨道插入）。直接测量：地表影像、成分图、地形。推断：地质活动（由撞击坑稀少、年轻地形推断）、地下海洋（没有直接证据，依据热模型）。Arrokoth（独立的柯伊伯带天体，而非冥王星卫星）：双叶形状约束形成情景（卵石云的引力坍缩），但形成事件并未被直接观测。
assignmentHtml.expected_output: 挑战T的详细比较材料，包括：各目标的观测表（观测→推断的过程→竞争性解释→具有区分力的证据）；区分着陆点测量与遥测；附URL的原始论文引用。

answerHtml:
COMPARISON DOSSIER: Huygens/Cassini at Titan vs New Horizons at Pluto and Arrokoth

=== SEPARATION OF MEASUREMENT TYPES ===

TITAN — LANDING-SITE (Huygens, Jan 14, 2005): Direct in situ measurements

  • DISR: Imaging and spectral radiometry during descent and at surface — drainage channels, rounded pebbles (water-ice composition), organic haze deposits
  • GCMS: Atmospheric composition profiles + post-landing surface volatile analysis — methane mole fraction 5.65% near surface; post-impact burst of CH4, C2H6, C2H2, C2N2 evaporation indicating surface liquid reservoirs (Niemann et al. 2010)
  • SSP: Acoustic sounder, accelerometer, tilt sensor — surface hardness/consistency (loose sand), deceleration profile at impact
  • HSI: In-situ temperature, pressure, wind, aerosol properties during descent

TITAN — REMOTE (Cassini orbiter): Regional/global measurements

  • RADAR (July 22, 2006 flyby): 75+ radar-dark patches interpreted as lakes via very low reflectivity + morphology (channels, topographic depressions) — Stofan et al. 2007
  • VIMS: Surface composition mapping (water ice, tholins, organics)
  • Broadband imaging: Global terrain context, seasonal changes

PLUTO — FLYBY ONLY (New Horizons, July 14, 2015): All remote, no landing

  • LORRI: High-resolution panchromatic imaging (5 μrad/pixel)
  • Ralph/MVIC: Color imaging in Blue/Red/CH4/NIR bands
  • Ralph/LEISA: Near-IR spectroscopic mapping (1.25–2.5 μm) for composition (N2, CH4, CO, H2O ice, organics)
  • PEPSSI/SWAP/Alice: Atmospheric escape, solar wind interaction
  • REX: Radio occultation for atmospheric profiles
  • All measurements are regional/global — no in situ contact

ARKOKOTH — FLYBY ONLY (New Horizons, Jan 1, 2019): All remote, no landing

  • Same instrument suite as Pluto encounter
  • Shape model from imaging: ~35 km long contact binary, two lenticular lobes aligned within 5°

=== FEATURE 1: CHANNELS (Titan landing site vs Pluto analogues) ===

TITAN — Channels at Huygens Landing Site

  • Observation: DISR images show branching network of narrow drainage channels running from brighter highlands to lower dark regions, merging into river systems with offshore 'islands' and 'shoals'; small rounded pebbles (up to 15 cm, water-ice composition per spectra) in dry riverbed (ESA Huygens highlights; Tomasko et al. 2005)
  • Inferred process: Fluvial erosion by liquid methane/ethane rainfall and runoff — Earth-like meteorology operating at -179°C where water is rock and methane is the condensable fluid
  • Competing explanations: (a) Dry granular flow by wind-blown organic haze particles; (b) Groundwater sapping without overland flow; (c) Debris flows of ice-rich material
  • Discriminating evidence: (1) Sinuous channel morphology with downstream widening consistent with channelized liquid flow (Burr et al. 2013); (2) Rounded pebbles 3 mm–15 cm size range consistent with fluvial transport abrasion; (3) Scour tails indicate energetic liquid action; (4) Fine-grained atmospheric aerosols cannot erode the observed valley networks (Burr et al. 2013); (5) GCMS detected methane precipitation signals and post-landing evaporation confirming liquid presence at surface (Niemann et al. 2010); (6) SSP showed loose, sand-like surface consistent with sediment transport by liquid (ESA Huygens highlights)

PLUTO — Channel-like features (no direct Titan-type channels)

  • Observation: Glaciers of nitrogen ice flowing from highlands into Sputnik Planitia, carving valleys; sublimation pits; water-ice 'icebergs' floating in N2 glacier (NASA 5-years-after page)
  • Inferred process: Solid-state glacial flow of volatile ices driven by thermal gradients; sublimation-erosion cycles
  • Competing: Liquid volatile flow (recent studies suggest possible transient liquid nitrogen/slush); cryovolcanic flooding
  • Discriminating evidence: Morphology matches solid-state glacial flow patterns; no evidence of liquid-phase channel incision at current temperatures

=== FEATURE 2: ACTIVE-LOOKING TERRAIN ===

TITAN — Active hydrological cycle

  • Observation: Seasonal lake filling/evaporation (varying lake fullness states — partly dry, liquid-filled, dry with rims); dark flood deposits on dried lake beds; changing shoreline positions across Cassini mission (Stofan et al. 2007; ESA Titan has liquid lakes page)
  • Inferred process: Active methane-based hydrological cycle — rainfall fills lakes, seasonal evaporation redistributes liquid across 29-year Saturn orbit cycle
  • Competing: Ancient relict lakes now dry; subsurface brine pockets; low-density dark deposit interpretation (ESA page notes this alternative but rules it out due to absence of wind-blown features)
  • Discriminating evidence: Multiple lakes in different fill states simultaneously; associated active-looking channel networks feeding lakes; radar brightness profiles consistent with liquid; GCMS confirmed methane precipitation and surface liquid at landing site (Niemann et al. 2010)

PLUTO — Geological activity (Sputnik Planitia)

  • Observation: Sputnik Planitia (~1,000 km wide) shows NO craters down to 2 km (low-res) or 625 m (high-res); polygonal convection cells (~10 km across) with warm centers/cold margins; glaciers flowing into basin; Wright Mons and Piccard Mons (cryovolcanic candidates) with central pits; enormous extensional faults up to 4 km deep (Moore et al. 2016; Trilling et al. 2016; NASA 5-years page)
  • Inferred process: Ongoing cryo-geophysical activity — convective overturn of nitrogen ice in Sputnik Planitia (<10 Myr surface age); possible cryovolcanism; tectonic activity from freezing subsurface ocean
  • Competing explanations: (a) Low impactor flux rather than resurfacing explains crater absence; (b) Viscous relaxation alone; (c) Old terrain preserved by chance; (d) For cryovolcanic features: glacial/tectonic uplift instead of extrusion
  • Discriminating evidence: (1) Crater depletion requires resurfacing <10 Myr given known KBO impactor flux — ruled out low-flux hypothesis (Trilling et al. 2016); (2) Convective viscosity constraints (~10^17 Pa-s) consistent with lab-measured N2 ice viscosity (~10^8 Pa-s), favoring convection model (Trilling et al. 2016); (3) Polygonal cell pattern matches convective cell geometry; (4) For cryovolcanic features: hummocky/ropey texture dissimilar to glacial-scoured terrain elsewhere on Pluto; features lie well above surroundings ruling out erosional remnants; paucity of craters implies constructional resurfacing (Singer et al. 2022)
  • SUBSURFACE OCEAN — Indirect only: Extensional tectonic faults indicate global expansion consistent with freezing ocean; thermal models show ice shell >260 km thick prevents ice-II formation (which would cause contraction); no direct observation possible (Hammond et al. 2016 via Brown University)

=== FEATURE 3: BILOBED SHAPE (Arrokoth) ===

ARKOKOTH — Bilobed Contact Binary

  • Observation: ~35 km long contact binary with two unequally sized lenticular lobes (22×20×7 km larger; 14×14×10 km smaller); flattening planes aligned within 5°; smooth lightly-cratered surface; uniform red color; albedo heterogeneity 5–12%; tentative water ice and methanol detections; no satellites, rings, or atmosphere (Stern et al. 2019; McKinnon et al. 2020)
  • Inferred process: Gravitational collapse of overdense pebble cloud in protosolar nebula → formation of co-orbiting binary → angular momentum loss (gas drag most effective for Arrokoth-scale bodies) → gentle low-velocity merger preserving pristine shape
  • Competing explanations: (a) Hierarchical accretion via catastrophic collisions between pre-existing planetesimals; (b) Spin instability/fission of rapidly rotating body; (c) Random chance collision of two independently formed bodies
  • Discriminating evidence: (1) Geometric alignment of lobe flattening planes (<5°) highly unlikely from random collision (McKinnon et al. 2020); (2) Collision simulations show impacts ≥ mutual escape velocity (~few m/s) would be highly damaging/destructive, inconsistent with pristine preservation; (3) Uniform color/composition indicates locally-sourced material (consistent with particle-cloud collapse) vs heterogeneous mixture expected from hierarchical accretion; (4) Low crater count indicates low collision rate environment, inconsistent with violent collisional history; (5) Flattened lenticular shapes and mounds ('raspberry-like' substructure of ~5 km diameter units) consistent with aggregation of similar-sized progenitors from same cloud (Eos.org Arrokoth mounds article); (6) NASA conclusion: "all but rule out hierarchical accretion" for Arrokoth specifically (NASA Arrokoth formation page)

=== KEY CONTRAST: DIRECT VS INDIRECT ===

Titan (Huygens): Only Solar System body besides Earth with an in situ probe landing. Direct measurement of atmospheric composition, surface volatiles, and physical properties at one point.

Pluto & Arrokoth (New Horizons): Flyby missions only — all measurements indirect (imaging, spectroscopy, particle counts at distance). Surface processes and interiors inferred from morphological analysis and thermal modeling.
